message.content:
The “great” schisms that most historians point to when discussing the major splits in Christian history are:

| # | Schism | Approximate Date | Key Parties Involved | Significance |
|---|--------|------------------|----------------------|--------------|
| 1 | **The Great Schism (East–West Schism)** | 1054 CE | Eastern (Byzantine) Church vs. Western (Roman) Church | Formal split between what are now the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic churches; lasting theological, liturgical, and political differences. |
| 2 | **The Protestant Reformation** | 1517–1648 CE | Roman Catholic Church vs. various reform movements (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, etc.) | Led to the creation of Protestant denominations, major doctrinal changes, and profound social‑political effects across Europe. |
| 3 | **The East–West Schism of 1965 (Ecumenical)** | 1965 CE | Eastern Orthodox Church vs. Roman Catholic Church (ecumenical dialogue) | While not a new split, this “schism” refers to the ongoing efforts and occasional setbacks in reconciling the two traditions, highlighting the enduring nature of the original divide. |

These three events are typically cited as the most consequential divisions that reshaped the structure, theology, and politics of Christianity over the centuries.
